docs.title: Cross integration: Multiple RNA + ADT¶
docs.text:
Cross integration combines batches that all measure the same modalities. The task is to remove batch effects and keep the biological structure. This tutorial is for batches that each hold RNA and ADT. It runs StabMap and sciPENN on D52mini, 3,000 cells in three batches of the benchmark dataset D52, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D52mini (2 MB) once. Each method runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for StabMap and sciPENN, with no conda needed. The download is 1.4 GB on a computer without a GPU and 3.0 GB on one with a GPU.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

Environments go to mtb.config.envs_dir. To use another disk, set it before this cell.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D52mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics and the classification scores (OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens, F1). res.summary has one row per method with its status, run time and scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

Each method writes an embedding: a table of numbers with one row per cell. run scores it against the cell-type labels of D52mini.

The clustering metrics ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI measure how well the embedding separates the cell types. The batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI measure how well the batches mix. They appear only when the data has several batches.

The reason column of res.summary says why a method failed. params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them. Many methods take none.

mtb.load_run("out/D52mini") reloads these results later without running anything.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

Details

The lightest fill is the lowest value in this figure, not zero.

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar. Its length and colour both show the family score.

A column whose rows all hold the same value is drawn grey, and a warning names it. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw RNA and ADT counts in one .h5ad file, with a cell type and a batch for each cell. ADT means the protein counts. A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. mtb.io.export_dataset with batch= writes one set of files per batch.

The methods of this task read three batches, and UINMF also reads two. The recipe for another number of donors covers the other cases.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file, no labels and another number of donors.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

The example keeps the protein names in adata.uns["protein_names"]. A DataFrame in adata.obsm["protein"] brings its own names in its columns.

The batches are numbered in the sorted order of their names, read as text: donors A, B and C become batches 1, 2 and 3, and 10 comes before 2.

For one AnnData per batch, call export_dataset once per batch with batch_index=N instead of batch=.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value. After batch=, the files of batch numbers that the call does not write count as well.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Stored results¶
docs.text:
The package ships stored results for 7 methods on D52. load_results reads them and mtb.plot.bubble draws them, without running anything.

Details

The stored results are for the full D52, the benchmark dataset D52mini is drawn from.

The stored results are the package's own runs of the methods.

Scores of your runs differ a little from the stored ones: most methods give a slightly different embedding on each run.

docs.title: Cross integration: Multiple RNA + ADT + ATAC¶
docs.text:
Cross integration combines batches that all measure the same modalities. The task is to remove batch effects and keep the biological structure. This tutorial is for batches that each hold RNA, ADT and ATAC peaks. It runs StabMap and UINMF on D59mini, 3,000 cells in two batches of the benchmark dataset D59, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D59mini (8 MB) once. Each method runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for StabMap and UINMF, with no conda needed. The download is 0.9 GB.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

Environments go to mtb.config.envs_dir. To use another disk, set it before this cell.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D59mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics and the classification scores (OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens, F1). res.summary has one row per method with its status, run time and scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

Each method writes an embedding: a table of numbers with one row per cell. run scores it against the cell-type labels of D59mini.

The clustering metrics ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI measure how well the embedding separates the cell types. The batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI measure how well the batches mix. They appear only when the data has several batches.

The reason column of res.summary says why a method failed. params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them. Many methods take none.

mtb.load_run("out/D59mini") reloads these results later without running anything.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

Details

The lightest fill is the lowest value in this figure, not zero.

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar. Its length and colour both show the family score.

A column whose rows all hold the same value is drawn grey, and a warning names it. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw RNA and ADT counts in one .h5ad file and an ATAC peak matrix of the same cells in another, with a cell type and a batch for each cell. ADT means the protein counts. A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. mtb.io.export_dataset with batch= writes one set of files per batch.

The methods of this task read two batches. The recipe for another number of donors covers the other cases.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file, no labels and another number of donors.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

The example keeps the protein names in adata.uns["protein_names"]. A DataFrame in adata.obsm["protein"] brings its own names in its columns.

The batches are numbered in the sorted order of their names, read as text: donors A, B and C become batches 1, 2 and 3, and 10 comes before 2.

For one AnnData per batch, call export_dataset once per batch with batch_index=N instead of batch=.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value. After batch=, the files of batch numbers that the call does not write count as well.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Every method of this task¶
docs.text:
5 methods have a variant for cross Multiple RNA + ADT + ATAC. Each ran on D59mini in the package's own check, on a server with a GPU:

Method Result Seconds MOFA2 scored 42 Multigrate scored 43 StabMap scored 13 UINMF scored 26 scMoMaT scored on the UMAP it writes 113

To run them all, set METHODS to these names in section 2 and run the notebook again. That downloads 4 envs, 15.8 GB to download on a CPU host, 15.5 GB on a GPU host. This notebook does the same in Colab.

docs.text:
res.summary[res.summary.status != "scored"] lists each method that failed or was skipped. Its reason column ends with the method's error output.

docs.title: Diagonal integration: [multiple RNA, multiple ATAC]¶
docs.text:
Diagonal integration combines RNA and ATAC measured in different cells, with no pairing between them. This tutorial is for data in several batches: three RNA batches and three ATAC batches. It runs iNMF and online_iNMF on D37mini, 3,000 RNA and 3,000 ATAC profiles of the benchmark dataset D37, then on data in your own format.

iNMF, online_iNMF and scJoint read ATAC as gene-activity scores, made beforehand with a tool such as Signac or ArchR. GLUE reads the peak matrix. The dataset holds both.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D37mini (12 MB) once. Each method runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for iNMF and online_iNMF, with no conda needed. The download is 0.9 GB.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

Environments go to mtb.config.envs_dir. To use another disk, set it before this cell.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D37mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics and the classification scores (OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens, F1). res.summary has one row per method with its status, run time and scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

Each method writes an embedding: a table of numbers with one row per cell. run scores it against the cell-type labels of D37mini.

The clustering metrics ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI measure how well the embedding separates the cell types. The batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI measure how well the batches mix. They appear only when the data has several batches.

The reason column of res.summary says why a method failed. params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them. Many methods take none.

mtb.load_run("out/D37mini") reloads these results later without running anything.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

Details

The lightest fill is the lowest value in this figure, not zero.

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar. Its length and colour both show the family score.

A column whose rows all hold the same value is drawn grey, and a warning names it. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw RNA counts and ATAC as one .h5ad file per batch, with a cell type for each cell. A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. mtb.io.export_dataset with batch_index= writes one RNA batch and one ATAC batch per call. iNMF and online_iNMF read ATAC as gene-activity scores, and online_iNMF needs about 5,000 cells in total. Gene-activity scores are an ATAC matrix with one column per gene, as Signac or ArchR compute it.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for labels in a CSV file and no labels.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

The RNA batches and the ATAC batches are numbered separately. RNA batch 1 and ATAC batch 1 need not come from the same sample. scJoint, GLUE, iNMF and online_iNMF read exactly three RNA and three ATAC batches. For another number, such as two donors, write one rna.h5 and one ATAC file with every cell, and pass the batches to run as batch=, one per RNA and ATAC cell, as in Another number of donors.

For ATAC as a peak matrix, pass atac_kind="peak". GLUE reads the peak matrix.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value. A call with batch_index= checks the files of its own batch number. Files of other batch numbers stay: for data with fewer batches, give NAME a new value.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Every method of this task¶
docs.text:
4 methods have a variant for diagonal [multiple RNA, multiple ATAC]. Each ran on D37mini in the package's own check, on a server with a GPU:

Method Result Seconds GLUE scored 567 iNMF scored 16 online_iNMF scored 8 scJoint scored 43

To run them all, set METHODS to these names in section 2 and run the notebook again. That downloads 3 envs, 4.8 GB to download on a CPU host, 8.3 GB on a GPU host. This notebook does the same in Colab.

The article also evaluates Conos on this task. Its published script reads a third input file in another format, so the package does not run it on more than two files.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text:
res.summary[res.summary.status != "scored"] lists each method that failed or was skipped. Its reason column ends with the method's error output.

Details symptom fix env.install refuses on macOS or Windows methods run only on Linux: use Colab or a Linux machine a method needs an NVIDIA GPU choose a GPU runtime on Colab, or a machine with a GPU a method fails on a small dataset mtb.scan names what the method needs from the data's size in its caveat column a warning that values are not whole numbers export raw counts, for example with rna="layer:counts" ... matrix/data as cells x features the matrix is transposed: export it again with mtb.io.export_dataset a method times out raise timeout= in run batch metrics use the wrong batches res.rescore(batch=my_vector) scores again without running the methods

docs.title: Diagonal integration: [RNA, ATAC]¶
docs.text:
Diagonal integration combines RNA and ATAC measured in different cells, with no pairing between them. If your RNA and ATAC come from the same cells, as in 10x Multiome, use the vertical tutorial. This tutorial runs iNMF and online_iNMF on D27mini, 3,000 RNA and 3,000 ATAC profiles of the benchmark dataset D27, then on data in your own format.

Most diagonal methods read ATAC as gene-activity scores, made beforehand with a tool such as Signac or ArchR. GLUE and Seurat_v5 read the peak matrix, and MultiMAP and Seurat_v3 need both. Seurat_v5 also needs RNA and ATAC from the same cells. The folder layout lists each method's ATAC files.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D27mini (15 MB) once. Each method runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for iNMF and online_iNMF, with no conda needed. The download is 0.9 GB.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

Environments go to mtb.config.envs_dir. To use another disk, set it before this cell.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D27mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics and the classification scores (OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens, F1). res.summary has one row per method with its status, run time and scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

Each method writes an embedding: a table of numbers with one row per cell. run scores it against the cell-type labels of D27mini.

The clustering metrics ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI measure how well the embedding separates the cell types. The batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI measure how well the batches mix. They appear only when the data has several batches.

The reason column of res.summary says why a method failed. params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them. Many methods take none.

mtb.load_run("out/D27mini") reloads these results later without running anything.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

Details

The lightest fill is the lowest value in this figure, not zero.

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar. Its length and colour both show the family score.

A column whose rows all hold the same value is drawn grey, and a warning names it. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw RNA counts in one .h5ad file and ATAC in another, with a cell type for each cell in both. iNMF and online_iNMF read ATAC as gene-activity scores, and online_iNMF needs about 5,000 cells in total. Gene-activity scores are an ATAC matrix with one column per gene, as Signac or ArchR compute it.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for labels in a CSV file and no labels.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

labels= needs the column in both files. With cell types for the RNA cells only, leave labels= out and follow the recipe for no labels.

For ATAC as a peak matrix, pass atac_kind="peak". GLUE and Seurat_v5 read peaks. The folder layout lists the files each method needs.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Stored results¶
docs.text:
The package ships stored results for 11 methods on D28. load_results reads them and mtb.plot.bubble draws them, without running anything.

Details

There are no stored results for D27mini. D28 is another benchmark dataset of the same task.

The stored results are the package's own runs of the methods.

Scores of your runs differ a little from the stored ones: most methods give a slightly different embedding on each run.

docs.title: 7. Every method of this task¶
docs.text:
14 methods have a variant for diagonal [RNA, ATAC]. Each ran on D27mini in the package's own check, on a server with a GPU:

Method Result Seconds Conos scored 42 GLUE scored 340 MultiMAP scored 23 Portal scored 44 SCALEX scored 261 Seurat_v3 scored 51 Seurat_v5 scored 357 VIPCCA scored 10 iNMF scored 18 online_iNMF scored 8 scBridge scored 26 scJoint scored 28 sciCAN scored 84 uniPort scored 463

To run them all, set METHODS to these names in section 2 and run the notebook again. That downloads 8 envs, 13.9 GB to download on a CPU host, 13.2 GB on a GPU host. This notebook does the same in Colab.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text:
res.summary[res.summary.status != "scored"] lists each method that failed or was skipped. Its reason column ends with the method's error output.

Details symptom fix env.install refuses on macOS or Windows methods run only on Linux: use Colab or a Linux machine a method needs an NVIDIA GPU choose a GPU runtime on Colab, or a machine with a GPU a method fails on a small dataset mtb.scan names what the method needs from the data's size in its caveat column a warning that values are not whole numbers export raw counts, for example with rna="layer:counts" ... matrix/data as cells x features the matrix is transposed: export it again with mtb.io.export_dataset a method times out raise timeout= in run batch metrics use the wrong batches res.rescore(batch=my_vector) scores again without running the methods

docs.title: Next steps¶
docs.text:
• The other tutorials: vertical RNA + ADT, vertical RNA + ATAC, vertical RNA + ADT + ATAC, diagonal [multiple RNA, multiple ATAC], mosaic [RNA, RNA + ADT, ADT], mosaic [RNA, RNA + ATAC, ATAC], mosaic Mixed, with shared modality, mosaic Mixed, without shared modality, cross Multiple RNA + ADT, cross Multiple RNA + ATAC, cross Multiple ADT + ATAC, cross Multiple RNA + ADT + ATAC.
  • The guides: run, evaluate, plot and discover methods.
  • The interactive explorer has the full benchmark's rankings, with no install needed.

docs.title: Discover methods
docs.text:
These calls show which of the 36 methods fit your data and your task. They need no environments, GPU or data.

Summary

import multibench as mtb

mtb.find_methods(category="vertical")   # every method in a category
# filter by what your data has
mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"],
                 needs_labels=False)
mtb.method_info("SCALEX")               # everything known about one method
# rank by the stored results
mtb.recommend("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"])

docs.title: The four integration categories
docs.text:
Pick the category that matches your experimental design and pass it as category= first. A method written for one design cannot take data from another.

Category Design Typical modalities vertical Several modalities measured in the same cells RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC diagonal Modalities measured in different cells, bridged by shared features RNA batch + ATAC batch mosaic Several batches, only some sharing a modality, joined by a paired batch mixed, partially paired cross Several batches, each with every modality RNA+ADT, RNA+ATAC, ADT+ATAC, RNA+ADT+ATAC

Several samples of 10x Multiome (RNA+ATAC) belong in vertical: one folder with all cells. To score batch mixing, pass each cell's sample as batch= to run or evaluate.

docs.title: Filter by what your data has
docs.text:
find_methods lists the methods, all 36 without a filter. Its filters are what your data has: the category, the modalities you measured, how your ATAC is encoded, and whether you have cell-type labels.

import multibench as mtb

mtb.find_methods()                       # all 36 methods
mtb.find_methods(category="vertical")    # paired-design methods only

Each method reads ATAC either as peaks or as gene activity. Give each method the representation it reads: atac_peak or atac_gas in modalities= keeps the methods that read yours.

# unpaired RNA and ATAC batches, no cell-type labels
mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["rna", "atac"],
                 needs_labels=False)
# ['SCALEX', 'Seurat_v5', 'VIPCCA', 'Portal', ...]

mtb.find_methods(category="diagonal", modalities=["atac_peak"])   # ATAC as peaks
Details

A method matches when one of its variants meets all the filters together. A variant is the version of a method for one category and one set of inputs. None, the default, turns a filter off.

modalities= keeps the variants that take every listed type, so ["rna"] is broad and ["rna", "atac"] stricter. "atac" matches any ATAC input, and protein means adt.

The other ATAC tokens select by what the method reads. "gas", "gene_activity" and "atac_gas" keep the methods that read gene activity. "peak" and "atac_peak" keep those that read peaks, including moETM, scMM and iPOLNG, whose input is named atac_gas. Naming both representations keeps MultiMAP and Seurat_v3, which read both files.

mtb.scan and run use the same tokens. They keep a row only when its modalities are exactly the listed ones, so scMoMaT's rna+adt+atac row is not kept for ["rna", "atac"]. A representation token keeps every row whose method reads it, so "atac_peak" also keeps MultiMAP and Seurat_v3.

needs_labels is judged per variant. method_info(m)["needs_labels"] is True when any variant needs labels. mtb.params_for(m, category, modalities) lists the hyperparameters a variant exposes.

An unknown token raises ValueError listing the valid values. A bare string such as modalities="rna" raises TypeError.

docs.title: My ATAC is peaks only
docs.text:
Most diagonal methods read gene activity. With a peak matrix alone, check which methods can run:

  • GLUE runs on peaks. It reads peak names such as chr1:100-200, and a run rewrites chr1_100_200 or chr1-100-200 into that form. It also needs the GENCODE annotation file. See Run a method.
  • Seurat_v5 needs a third dataset: a paired bridge with RNA and ATAC from the same cells. The package passes your RNA and ATAC files as that bridge, so it cannot run on unpaired data here.
  • MultiMAP and Seurat_v3 also need gene activity for the same ATAC cells.
  • The other ten need gene activity instead of peaks, for the ATAC cells of atac_peak.h5. Make it outside the package, for example with Signac GeneActivity, read it into an AnnData gas, and write it into the folder with mtb.io.export_dataset(gas, "data/X", rna=None, atac="X", atac_kind="gene_activity", category="diagonal").

mtb.scan then shows which methods have their files.

Details

mtb.scan compares the cells of atac_gas.h5 with those of atac_peak.h5. Other cells, or the same cells in another order, fail the file check. Barcodes that differ only in a suffix such as -1 or -2 count as the same cell.

export_dataset writes the rows in the cell order of the folder's atac_peak.h5, which atac_cty.csv follows, and refuses other cells.

docs.title: Inspect a single method
docs.text:
method_info returns what the package knows about one method.

info = mtb.method_info("SCALEX")
info["env"], info["atac"], info["needs_labels"]
# ('scmb_torch', 'gene_activity', False)
info["supports"]    # one entry per variant: category, modalities, labels, ...
info["runtime"]     # {..., 'tier': 'slow', 'worst_sec': 2233, ...}
Details

runtime["observed"] lists measured runs, with dataset, cells and seconds, and tier summarises them from fast to very_slow. Use it to set run(timeout=...). On a CPU, training methods take much longer than these times.

info["setup_hint"] names what a method needs before its first run, such as GLUE's annotation file. setup_hint is empty for most methods. mtb.params_for(method) lists what run(params=...) can change and what the script fixes.

Unknown method ids raise KeyError with a did-you-mean hint. Every function takes a method id in any case, and the article's spellings such as MOFA+.

The keys of method_info are listed in its reference entry. gpu says how a method uses an NVIDIA GPU: required, used when present, not used or unknown. cpu_params holds the flags that turn CUDA off, which a run adds on a computer without a GPU.

docs.title: Rank from stored results
docs.text:
recommend ranks a category's methods by their stored results, in the order of the figures.

mtb.recommend("vertical", modalities=["rna", "adt"])
#   method  grand_score  needs_labels  runtime_tier  worst_sec  env
mtb.recommend("diagonal", modalities=["atac_peak"])   # only methods that read peaks
mtb.recommend("vertical", methods=mtb.find_methods("vertical", needs_labels=False))

grand_score compares a category's methods with each other. On each dataset, each metric ranks a method's value among the stored methods' values. The mean of a method's ranks is min-max scaled, so that the best stored method gets 1 and the lowest 0, and your own rows are placed on that scale. grand_score is the mean over the datasets a method was scored on. It is a rank, not a quality score.

The stored results cover one dataset per category: for vertical, D11. Read the ranking as a hint. The full benchmark ranking is in the interactive explorer and in Fig. 6 of the paper. Methods with needs_labels=True train on your cell types, so compare them only with each other.

Details

The Seurat_v5 script reads its bridge as two extra files. Its stored diagonal scores come from runs with a separate paired bridge dataset. They do not mean that it runs on your unpaired folder.

To rank your own method alongside, pass long_df=pd.concat([mtb.load_results(category), mine]).

Methods that fit the category but have no stored results are listed last, with grand_score NaN. modalities= naming a modality that no ranked dataset measured raises.

modalities= follows the find_methods rule above. It only shortens the list, so a filtered list can start below 1 and end above 0.

metrics= picks the metric family. The default ranks on every metric present, as the figures do. needs_labels follows the category's variants.

docs.title: The full benchmark catalog
docs.text:
mtb.catalog returns the dataset and metric tables as DataFrames.

mtb.catalog.datasets()    # the fetchable datasets: category, has_results
mtb.catalog.metrics()     # each metric with its family and what it measures
Details

The rows are the benchmark's datasets and the demo subsets mtb.data.fetch downloads. has_results marks the datasets with stored results.

docs.title: Before running
docs.text:
Check your folder with mtb.scan("MYDATA", category). It says, per method, whether it can run here and why not, and gives the command run would execute. Then run them with mtb.run.

By default scan lists the methods that read the modalities the folder holds, and modalities="all" lists every method.

Next: run a chosen method in Run a method, score it in Evaluate a run, and compare methods in Load and plot results.

docs.title: End-to-end walkthrough¶
docs.text:
This notebook takes one method through each step: find it, check its parameters, install its environment, run it on a dataset, score its embedding and plot the scores. The method is Matilda and the dataset is D11: 2,864 blood cells measured with CITE-seq, which gives RNA and surface protein (ADT) for each cell.

find_methods → params_for → env.install → run → evaluate → plot.bubble

The category tutorials run several methods at once with the same run. Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Find a method¶
docs.text: find_methods lists the methods that fit a category and a set of modalities. method_info describes one of them.

docs.title: 3. Get the data¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D11 (11 MB) once. scan says whether Matilda can run on it here, and why not.

Details

A dataset folder of your own works the same way. mtb.io.export_dataset writes one from an AnnData, as the category tutorials show.

docs.title: 4. Check the parameters¶
docs.text:
params_for lists the options of Matilda's script under tunable, with the default a run uses. Section 6 changes one with params=.

Details

Many methods take no parameters from the command line, and their tunable is empty.

The params_for reference lists the other keys.

docs.title: 5. Install the environment¶
docs.text:
Matilda runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads it, with no conda needed. The download is 0.6 GB on a computer without a GPU and 3.0 GB on one with a GPU.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

docs.title: 6. Run¶
docs.text:
run runs Matilda on D11, scores its embedding and saves the result under out/. params={"Matilda": {"epochs": 10}} shortens training for this demo. res.embedding("Matilda") returns the embedding as an AnnData: one row per cell, named by its barcode, with its cell type in obs["label"].

Details

res.summary has the status and the scores of the run, and its reason column says why a method failed.

mtb.scan("D11", "vertical", methods=["Matilda"]) returns the plan and the command without running anything. It works on any computer.

docs.title: 7. Score¶
docs.text:
evaluate scores the embedding against the cell types in emb.obs["label"] and returns a long table, one row per metric. method= and dataset= name the rows.

Details

metrics="clustering" computes ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI. D11 has a single batch, so the batch metrics do not apply.

For an embedding file, mtb.evaluate(path, dataset="D11", category="vertical", method="Matilda") matches the dataset's label files to the cells by the barcodes run writes into the file.

Scores of this run differ a little from the stored ones: most methods give a slightly different embedding on each run.

docs.title: 8. Plot¶
docs.text:
The cell adds this run to the package's stored results of D11 and plots them together.

Details

Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

The stored results cover one dataset per category. Rows from your own dataset go in a figure of their own.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
step API find a method find_methods, method_info get the data data.fetch, scan check the parameters params_for install the environment mtb.env.install run run(..., methods=[...], params={...}), embedding score evaluate plot load_results, plot.bubble

The category tutorials (vertical, diagonal, mosaic, cross) run and score several methods in one call, on the demo data and on your own.

docs.title: Evaluate a run
docs.text:
mtb.evaluate scores an embedding against cell-type labels with the article's metrics and returns them as a long table. An embedding is a table with one row per cell, like adata.obsm["X_pca"].

Summary

import scanpy as sc
import multibench as mtb

mtb.data.fetch("D11")
mtb.data.write_example("D11")     # my_file.h5ad: cell types in obs["celltype"]
adata = sc.read_h5ad("my_file.h5ad")
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.pca(adata)                  # the embedding to score: adata.obsm["X_pca"]
scores = mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca", method="PCA",
                      category="vertical", metrics="clustering")
print(scores)

docs.title: Choose the metrics
docs.text:
metrics= takes a family ("clustering", "batch", "classification", "all"), a metric code, or a list of codes and families. The default computes every metric your inputs allow except kBET.

mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca", metrics="cLISI")
mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca", metrics=["ARI", "NMI"])

The protocol is the article's. ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW and iF1 score Leiden clusters searched to the number of cell types. ARI_batch and NMI_batch score Leiden clusters searched to the number of batches.

Details

The search bisects the Leiden resolution on [0, 3] for at most 30 steps until the clustering has the number of clusters wanted. When no step gets there, the last step's clusters are scored. The clusters come from scanpy's default 15-neighbour graph of the embedding, or of its first 50 principal components when it is wider, as in the article. cLISI, iLISI and GC use the 15-neighbour graph of the whole embedding.

A selection without the seven metrics above skips the search, such as metrics="cLISI".

kBET is computed only when a list names it, and can take hours on large datasets.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Pass the embedding and one cell-type label per cell, in the embedding's row order. Both can be paths or in-memory objects. The reference lists the accepted forms.

# embedding and labels in one AnnData
mtb.evaluate(adata, labels="celltype", obsm="X_pca")

A column is named with or without obs:, so labels="obs:celltype" is the same. The labels of a dataset folder, in its cell order:

import pandas as pd
folder = mtb.data.fetch("D52mini")
order = {"rna": 0, "adt": 1, "atac": 2}
files = sorted(folder.glob("*cty*.csv"),
               key=lambda f: (order.get(f.stem.split("_")[0], -1), len(f.stem), f.stem))
labels = pd.concat([pd.read_csv(f).iloc[:, 0] for f in files]).to_numpy()

They follow the folder's cells as mtb.io.read_canonical reads them: RNA before ADT before ATAC, batches by number. A method's output may order its cells otherwise: score it with evaluate(dataset=, category=, method=) and no labels=. The embedding.h5 that run writes names its cells, and evaluate matches the label files to them.

A missing label is not a cell type: evaluate raises when a label is missing, and so does a missing batch. Score the labelled cells, as adata[adata.obs["celltype"].notna()].

Details

labels takes a CSV path with a header row (column x, or the only column), a list of CSV paths stacked in that order, a 1-D array or Series, or the name of an .obs column. batch takes the same forms.

With an AnnData, labels and batch can name .obs columns, and obsm= names the embedding. A MuData works the same way, with the joint embedding in its .obsm, and "rna:celltype" names a column of one modality.

A label is missing when it is NaN, None, blank text, or text that a label file reads as missing, such as NA, nan or null.

When the output has cell ids (an AnnData, an .h5ad file, a DataFrame indexed by cell id, or a CSV embedding whose first column holds the barcodes), the ids decide. A Series indexed by cell id is aligned by id. A CSV whose first column holds the cell ids is aligned the same way. Ids of other cells are left out. A label file without cell ids in a dataset folder takes the cell ids of the matrix next to it. Any other file or Series without cell ids is refused: add the barcodes, or pass .to_numpy() to match by position. When the output is a bare array, it has no cell ids: a Series, and a CSV whose first column holds cell ids, are matched by position, with a warning. Plain arrays, lists and a CSV without cell ids are always matched by position.

docs.title: Batch metrics
docs.text:
Batch metrics also need one batch per cell. Pass batch=, or dataset= of a multi-batch dataset folder without labels: each of its label files is then a batch. Give the category and the method too, so the files follow the rows of the method's output. A wrong order gives wrong scores without an error.

mtb.data.fetch("D52mini")
mtb.data.write_example("D52mini", "d52")   # d52/my_file.h5ad: donors in obs["batch"]
cross = sc.read_h5ad("d52/my_file.h5ad")
sc.pp.normalize_total(cross)
sc.pp.log1p(cross)
sc.pp.pca(cross)
mtb.evaluate(cross, labels="celltype", batch="batch", obsm="X_pca", metrics="all")
Details

A run's embedding.h5 holds the name of each cell (the dataset barcodes), so dataset= matches the label files to its cells whatever method= says. In a run folder written before 0.4.0, the run's record names the method that made the file. For an embedding without cell names, dataset= reads the cell order of method= when it names a package method, also as method="StabMap (this run)", else the folder's order: numbered files ascending, and rna before adt before atac. StabMap puts its reference batch first, which is cty3 on D52. Without category=, a benchmark dataset gives it. On a folder of your own, a package method needs it. A list of label files is stacked in the order given.

ARI_batch and NMI_batch are 1 minus the absolute ARI and NMI between the batch clusters and the batches, so higher means better mixed batches.

Without batch=, run uses each cell's label file as its batch, so batches inside one file, such as donors, are not scored. Pass batch= to run, or re-score saved outputs with the real batch vector, mtb.load_run("out/").rescore(batch=...). No method is re-run.

docs.title: Classification metrics
docs.text:
With two or more batches, evaluate also predicts each cell's type from another batch and scores the predictions: OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens and F1. The default adds them unless category="vertical".

mtb.evaluate(cross, labels="celltype", batch="batch", obsm="X_pca",
             metrics="classification")
Details

Each batch in turn is the reference that a small neural network learns from, as in the article. The scores are the mean over the references, as the article reports them.

They need the method's embedding. A graph method has none, and run leaves them out for it. Where they cannot be computed, metrics="classification" raises. "all" gives NaN with a warning, and so does the default, except on data in one batch, where it leaves them out.

For vertical data in several batches, ask for them with metrics="classification".

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
evaluate returns the long table: one row per metric, with the columns metric, value, method, dataset, category, source and scored_with. method=, dataset= and category= fill their columns, and source reads user. A metric that cannot run on your machine is NaN, with a warning.

scores.to_csv("mine.csv", index=False)
scores.pivot(index="method", columns="metric", values="value")

Add your own method concatenates it with the stored results.

docs.title: What each metric measures
docs.text:
All metrics are scaled so that higher is better. Most lie between 0 and 1. ARI can be slightly below 0, which means a random clustering.

Metric Family What it measures ARI clustering How well the Leiden clusters match the cell types NMI clustering How much the Leiden clusters tell about the cell types ASW clustering How well the Leiden clusters separate from each other iASW clustering ASW averaged per Leiden cluster, each cluster counted as isolated iF1 clustering How well one Leiden cluster captures each cell type cLISI clustering How much each cell's neighbours share its cell type ASW_batch batch How well the batches mix within each cell type ARI_batch batch How little the batch clusters match the batches NMI_batch batch How little the batch clusters tell about the batches GC batch How much of each cell type stays in one connected group of neighbours iLISI batch How many batches appear among each cell's neighbours kBET batch How often a neighbourhood holds the overall batch mix OCA classification The fraction of query cells predicted correctly ACA classification The fraction of each cell type predicted correctly, averaged over cell types Spec classification Specificity, averaged over cell types Sens classification Sensitivity, averaged over cell types F1 classification F1-score, averaged over cell types

mtb.catalog.metrics() describes each metric in one line. The details below give the exact computation.

Details

cLISI and iLISI need scib's compiled LISI helper. Where the binary scib ships cannot run, evaluate rebuilds it once if a C++ compiler (g++, c++ or clang++) is on PATH. Otherwise the warning prints the build command.

kBET needs R through rpy2. Otherwise kBET is NaN.

Each metric is a scib function on the embedding. The package needs scib 1.1 or newer, and attrs["scib_version"] records the version.

code       scib function         arguments
ARI, NMI   ari, nmi              clusters, one per cell type
ASW        silhouette            those clusters, rescaled to 0-1
iASW       isolated_labels_asw   those clusters, every label isolated
iF1        isolated_labels_f1    cell types, best F1 of one cluster
cLISI      clisi_graph           90 nearest cells by path on the
                                 15-neighbour graph, scaled to 0-1
ASW_batch  silhouette_batch      1 - |batch silhouette| per cell type
ARI_batch  ari                   1 - |ARI| of clusters, one per batch
NMI_batch  nmi                   1 - |NMI|, the same way
GC         graph_connectivity    the 15-neighbour graph
iLISI      ilisi_graph           as cLISI, for the batches
kBET       kBET                  only when a list names it

Every label counts as isolated (iso_threshold = number of batches + 1). scib's default counts only labels found in few batches.

cLISI and iLISI take the median m of the per-cell scores and scale it: cLISI = (L - m)/(L - 1) and iLISI = (m - 1)/(B - 1), with L cell types and B batches.

docs.title: Look at an embedding
docs.text:
res.embedding(method) returns a method's embedding as an AnnData, with the cell types in obs["label"]. Three scanpy lines draw its UMAP:

import scanpy as sc

e = res.embedding("Matilda")          # or mtb.load_run("out/").embedding("Matilda")
sc.pp.neighbors(e, use_rep="X_emb"); sc.tl.umap(e); sc.pl.umap(e, color="label")

When the dataset folder was written from your AnnData, the cells' names are its obs_names, and one line puts the embedding into it: adata.obsm["X_Matilda"] = e[adata.obs_names].obsm["X_emb"].

docs.title: Are my numbers comparable?
docs.text:
Score a method's output with the dataset's own labels, in the method's cell order: mtb.evaluate(embedding, dataset=..., category=..., method=...).

Scores of your runs differ a little from the stored ones: most methods give a slightly different embedding on each run. The Leiden-based and classification scores of the same embedding also depend on the cells' order.

Details

The scored_with column records how the scores were computed: the Leiden backend, where the clusters came from and the multibench version, such as leidenalg/search/0.4.0.

Next: draw it next to the stored results in Load and plot results.

docs.title: Mosaic integration: [RNA, RNA + ADT, ADT]¶
docs.text:
Mosaic integration combines batches that share only some modalities. Each method accepts one batch pattern. This tutorial is for an RNA batch, an RNA + ADT batch and an ADT batch. It runs StabMap and scMoMaT on D38mini, 6,000 cells of the benchmark dataset D38, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D38mini (2 MB) once. Each method runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for StabMap and scMoMaT, with no conda needed. The download is 1.8 GB on a computer without a GPU and 5.4 GB on one with a GPU.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

Environments go to mtb.config.envs_dir. To use another disk, set it before this cell.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D38mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics and the classification scores (OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens, F1). scMoMaT writes a graph, so it gets no classification scores. res.summary has one row per method with its status, run time and scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

Each method writes an embedding: a table of numbers with one row per cell. run scores it against the cell-type labels of D38mini.

The clustering metrics ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI measure how well the embedding separates the cell types. The batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI measure how well the batches mix. They appear only when the data has several batches.

scMoMaT writes a graph instead of an embedding. run scores its UMAP.

The reason column of res.summary says why a method failed. params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them. Many methods take none.

mtb.load_run("out/D38mini") reloads these results later without running anything.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

Details

The lightest fill is the lowest value in this figure, not zero.

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar. Its length and colour both show the family score.

A column whose rows all hold the same value is drawn grey, and a warning names it. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw counts, with one .h5ad file per batch and modality and a cell type for each cell. A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. mtb.io.export_dataset with batch_index= writes one batch per call. Number the batches as below: RNA, then RNA + ADT, then ADT. ADT means the protein counts.

Every RNA file needs the same gene names and every ADT file the same protein names, in the same order. scMoMaT matches the features of two batches by position, and the check does not compare their names across batches.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file and no labels.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

The folder layout lists the batch patterns and the methods that accept each one.

A batch with RNA and ADT in one file goes in with a selector, for example adt="obsm:protein".

When the ADT file also holds a matrix in obsm under a name that does not start with X_, export_dataset asks which one is the protein matrix. X_umap and X_pca are left alone.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value. A call with batch_index= checks the files of its own batch number. Files of other batch numbers stay: for data with fewer batches, give NAME a new value.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Every method of this task¶
docs.text:
3 methods have a variant for mosaic [RNA, RNA + ADT, ADT]. Each ran on D38mini in the package's own check, on a server with a GPU:

Method Result Seconds Multigrate scored 101 StabMap scored 11 scMoMaT scored on the UMAP it writes 126

To run them all, set METHODS to these names in section 2 and run the notebook again. That downloads 3 envs, 6.2 GB to download on a CPU host, 5.9 GB on a GPU host. This notebook does the same in Colab.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶

docs.title: Mosaic integration: [RNA, RNA + ATAC, ATAC]¶
docs.text:
Mosaic integration combines batches that share only some modalities. Each method accepts one batch pattern, and every mosaic method reads ATAC as peaks. This tutorial is for an RNA batch, an RNA + ATAC batch and an ATAC batch. It runs StabMap and scMoMaT on D45mini, 6,000 cells of the benchmark dataset D45, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D45mini (11 MB) once. Each method runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for StabMap and scMoMaT, with no conda needed. The download is 1.8 GB on a computer without a GPU and 5.4 GB on one with a GPU.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

Environments go to mtb.config.envs_dir. To use another disk, set it before this cell.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D45mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics and the classification scores (OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens, F1). scMoMaT writes a graph, so it gets no classification scores. res.summary has one row per method with its status, run time and scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

Each method writes an embedding: a table of numbers with one row per cell. run scores it against the cell-type labels of D45mini.

The clustering metrics ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI measure how well the embedding separates the cell types. The batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI measure how well the batches mix. They appear only when the data has several batches.

scMoMaT writes a graph instead of an embedding. run scores its UMAP.

The reason column of res.summary says why a method failed. params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them. Many methods take none.

mtb.load_run("out/D45mini") reloads these results later without running anything.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

Details

The lightest fill is the lowest value in this figure, not zero.

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar. Its length and colour both show the family score.

A column whose rows all hold the same value is drawn grey, and a warning names it. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw counts, with one .h5ad file per batch and modality and a cell type for each cell. A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. mtb.io.export_dataset with batch_index= writes one batch per call. Number the batches as below: RNA, then RNA + ATAC, then ATAC. Give ATAC as peaks.

Every RNA file needs the same gene names and every ATAC file the same peaks, in the same order. scMoMaT matches the features of two batches by position, and the check does not compare their names across batches.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file and no labels.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

The folder layout lists the batch patterns and the methods that accept each one.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value. A call with batch_index= checks the files of its own batch number. Files of other batch numbers stay: for data with fewer batches, give NAME a new value.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Stored results¶
docs.text:
The package ships stored results for 4 methods on D45. load_results reads them and mtb.plot.bubble draws them, without running anything.

Details

The stored results are for the full D45, the benchmark dataset D45mini is drawn from.

The stored results are the package's own runs of the methods.

Scores of your runs differ a little from the stored ones: most methods give a slightly different embedding on each run.

docs.title: 7. Every method of this task¶
docs.text:
6 methods have a variant for mosaic [RNA, RNA + ATAC, ATAC]. Each ran on D45mini in the package's own check, on a server with a GPU:

Method Result Seconds Cobolt scored 119 MultiVI scored 292 Multigrate scored 106 SMILE scored 48 StabMap scored 14 scMoMaT scored on the UMAP it writes 92

To run them all, set METHODS to these names in section 2 and run the notebook again. That downloads 6 envs, 7.6 GB to download on a CPU host, 8.9 GB on a GPU host. This notebook does the same in Colab.

docs.title: Mosaic integration: Mixed, with shared modality¶
docs.text:
Mosaic integration combines batches that share only some modalities. Each method accepts one batch pattern, and every mosaic method reads ATAC as peaks. This tutorial is for an RNA + ADT batch, an RNA + ATAC batch and an RNA batch, so every batch holds RNA. It runs StabMap and UINMF on D46mini, 4,500 cells of the benchmark dataset D46, and then on data in your own format.

Methods run on Linux. On macOS or Windows, open this notebook in Colab.

docs.title: 1. Install¶
docs.text:
This cell installs multibench-sc. It keeps the numpy and pandas that are already installed, so Colab needs no restart.

Details

On Colab, choose a GPU runtime before you run the notebook: Runtime -> Change runtime type -> T4 GPU. On a CPU runtime, an environment that has a smaller CPU build gets that build, and training methods run slower.

docs.title: 2. Download the data and the environments¶
docs.text:
mtb.data.fetch downloads D46mini (4 MB) once. Each method runs in its own environment. mtb.env.install downloads the environments for StabMap and UINMF, with no conda needed. The download is 0.9 GB.

Details

state is PACKED for an environment downloaded now and have for one that was already there. With dry_run=True, mtb.env.install downloads nothing and returns the plan with its sizes.

Environments go to mtb.config.envs_dir. To use another disk, set it before this cell.

docs.title: 3. Run the methods¶
docs.text:
run runs each method on D46mini and scores its output with the scIB metrics and the classification scores (OCA, ACA, Spec, Sens, F1). res.summary has one row per method with its status, run time and scores. Higher is better for every metric.

Details

Each method writes an embedding: a table of numbers with one row per cell. run scores it against the cell-type labels of D46mini.

The clustering metrics ARI, NMI, ASW, iASW, iF1 and cLISI measure how well the embedding separates the cell types. The batch metrics ASW_batch, ARI_batch, NMI_batch, GC and iLISI measure how well the batches mix. They appear only when the data has several batches.

The reason column of res.summary says why a method failed. params={"Method": {"key": value}} sets a method's parameters, and mtb.params_for lists them. Many methods take none.

mtb.load_run("out/D46mini") reloads these results later without running anything.

docs.title: 4. Plot¶
docs.text:
res.plot() draws the scores as a bubble table. Circle size shows the rank within a column, and bigger is better. The fill compares a value with the other rows in the same column.

Details

The lightest fill is the lowest value in this figure, not zero.

Metrics are grouped by family: blue for clustering, green for batch correction, pink for classification. Each family starts with an Overall bar. Its length and colour both show the family score.

A column whose rows all hold the same value is drawn grey, and a warning names it. A figure of one method is grey everywhere.

docs.title: 5. Your own data¶
docs.text:
Your data needs raw counts, with one .h5ad file per batch and modality and a cell type for each cell. A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. mtb.io.export_dataset with batch_index= writes one batch per call. Number the batches as below: RNA + ADT, then RNA + ATAC, then RNA. Give ATAC as peaks. ADT means the protein counts.

Every RNA file needs the same gene names, in the same order. scMoMaT matches the features of two batches by position, and the check does not compare their names across batches.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file and no labels.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

The folder layout lists the batch patterns and the methods that accept each one.

A batch with RNA and ADT in one file goes in with a selector, for example adt="obsm:protein".

When the ADT file also holds a matrix in obsm under a name that does not start with X_, export_dataset asks which one is the protein matrix. X_umap and X_pca are left alone.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value. A call with batch_index= checks the files of its own batch number. Files of other batch numbers stay: for data with fewer batches, give NAME a new value.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Every method of this task¶
docs.text:
4 methods have a variant for mosaic Mixed, with shared modality. Each ran on D46mini in the package's own check, on a server with a GPU:

Method Result Seconds Multigrate scored 103 StabMap scored 12 UINMF scored 24 scMoMaT scored on the UMAP it writes 128

To run them all, set METHODS to these names in section 2 and run the notebook again. That downloads 3 envs, 6.2 GB to download on a CPU host, 5.9 GB on a GPU host. This notebook does the same in Colab.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text:
res.summary[res.summary.status != "scored"] lists each method that failed or was skipped. Its reason column ends with the method's error output.

Details symptom fix env.install refuses on macOS or Windows methods run only on Linux: use Colab or a Linux machine a method needs an NVIDIA GPU choose a GPU runtime on Colab, or a machine with a GPU a method fails on a small dataset mtb.scan names what the method needs from the data's size in its caveat column a warning that values are not whole numbers export raw counts, for example with rna="layer:counts" ... matrix/data as cells x features the matrix is transposed: export it again with mtb.io.export_dataset a method times out raise timeout= in run batch metrics use the wrong batches res.rescore(batch=my_vector) scores again without running the methods

docs.text:
Your data needs raw counts, with one .h5ad file per batch and modality and a cell type for each cell. A batch is a donor, a sample or an experiment. mtb.io.export_dataset with batch_index= writes one batch per call. Number the batches as below: RNA + ADT, then RNA + ATAC, then ADT. Give ATAC as peaks. ADT means the protein counts.

Every RNA file needs the same gene names and every ADT file the same protein names, in the same order. scMoMaT matches the features of two batches by position, and the check does not compare their names across batches.

Starting from something else? See the recipes for a 10x .h5 file, labels in a CSV file and no labels.

Details: export

The names in quotes say where your file holds each part. "X" is the main matrix, "obsm:protein" the matrix obsm["protein"], "layer:counts" the layer layers["counts"], and "obs:celltype" the column obs["celltype"], which "celltype" alone names too. A wrong name after obsm:, layer: or obs: raises an error that lists the names the file has.

The folder layout lists the batch patterns and the methods that accept each one.

A batch with RNA and ADT in one file goes in with a selector, for example adt="obsm:protein".

When the ADT file also holds a matrix in obsm under a name that does not start with X_, export_dataset asks which one is the protein matrix. X_umap and X_pca are left alone.

"mydata/" + NAME is the dataset folder that scan and run read. With a new value of NAME, the folder holds the files of your data only.

The check lists the methods you name. Without methods=, it lists every method that reads the modalities in the folder. Its command column holds the line run would execute for each method.

export_dataset raises FileExistsError when the folder holds files of other cells that the call does not write. overwrite=True does not remove them. Give NAME a new value. A call with batch_index= checks the files of its own batch number. Files of other batch numbers stay: for data with fewer batches, give NAME a new value.

overwrite=True replaces the files of an earlier run of this cell. Without it, export_dataset raises FileExistsError rather than replace a file.

docs.title: 6. Every method of this task¶
docs.text:
3 methods have a variant for mosaic Mixed, without shared modality. Each ran on D49mini in the package's own check, on a server with a GPU:

Method Result Seconds Multigrate scored 109 StabMap scored 11 scMoMaT scored on the UMAP it writes 104

To run them all, set METHODS to these names in section 2 and run the notebook again. That downloads 3 envs, 6.2 GB to download on a CPU host, 5.9 GB on a GPU host. This notebook does the same in Colab.

docs.title: Troubleshooting¶
docs.text:
res.summary[res.summary.status != "scored"] lists each method that failed or was skipped. Its reason column ends with the method's error output.

Details symptom fix env.install refuses on macOS or Windows methods run only on Linux: use Colab or a Linux machine a method needs an NVIDIA GPU choose a GPU runtime on Colab, or a machine with a GPU a method fails on a small dataset mtb.scan names what the method needs from the data's size in its caveat column a warning that values are not whole numbers export raw counts, for example with rna="layer:counts" ... matrix/data as cells x features the matrix is transposed: export it again with mtb.io.export_dataset a method times out raise timeout= in run batch metrics use the wrong batches res.rescore(batch=my_vector) scores again without running the methods
